items.title: SGLang v0.5.18 — cold starts get 2.38x faster, seven model families land
items.summary: SGLang v0.5.18 stages model weights from storage while CUDA graphs capture, so a Qwen3-32B server on an H100 starts in 35.6 seconds instead of 84.8. Seven new model families get serving support. 710 pull requests from 212 contributors.

quickFacts.label: New model families
quickFacts.value: Muse Glimmer, Intern-S2-Mobius, SANA-Video, LingBot-Video-MoE, LTX-2.5, Cosmos3 Edge & Distilled, LongCat-Image

quickFacts.label: Breaking change
quickFacts.value: All compiled-kernel caches move under SGLANG_CACHE_DIR

faq.q: Is the faster startup path in SGLang v0.5.18 on by default?
faq.a: No. The overlapped checkpoint staging in SGLang v0.5.18 is opt-in — pass --startup-weight-load-mode overlap when you launch the server. Against a serial load that already prefetches, the overlap mode saves 8.6 to 11.7 percent on Qwen3-32B on an H100. Against the plain default it is 2.38 times faster.

faq.q: What breaks when I upgrade to SGLang v0.5.18?
faq.a: SGLang v0.5.18 moves the Triton, FlashInfer, Inductor, DeepGEMM and CUDA driver caches into one directory controlled by SGLANG_CACHE_DIR. The old caches are no longer read, so the first launch after upgrading recompiles kernels once and takes longer than usual. Later launches reuse the new directory normally.

faq.q: Which GPUs benefit from the FlashInfer allreduce change?
faq.a: The pure-allreduce path in SGLang v0.5.18 reuses the FlashInfer MNNVL workspace instead of falling back to NCCL, and the measured gain is on Blackwell — DeepSeek-V4-Flash decode at TP4 improves up to 6.9 percent at small batch sizes. SGLang turns it on automatically for DeepSeek V3, V3.2 and V4; elsewhere use --enable-flashinfer-pure-allreduce.

faq.q: How does SGLang v0.5.18 differ from v0.5.17?
faq.a: Version 0.5.17 was about day-0 coverage for two frontier open models, Kimi K3 and MiniMax H3, across 582 pull requests. SGLang v0.5.18 is larger at 710 pull requests and aims at overhead instead — startup time, decode-step cost and one cache directory — while adding seven mostly multimodal and diffusion model families.

explainer.tagline: SGLang v0.5.18 overlaps weight loading with CUDA graph capture, cutting a large-model cold start from 85 seconds to 36.
explainer.whatIsIt: Overlapped checkpoint staging is the headline change in SGLang v0.5.18. The server used to read model weights off storage and then capture CUDA graphs; now the two run at the same time. On an H100 serving Qwen3-32B that turns an 84.8-second cold start into 35.6 seconds. The release also adds serving recipes for seven new model families, most of them multimodal or diffusion — Muse Glimmer, Intern-S2-Mobius, SANA-Video, LingBot-Video-MoE, LTX-2.5, Cosmos3 Edge and Distilled, and LongCat-Image.
explainer.howItWorks: Three separate overheads get trimmed. Checkpoint pages stage from storage in parallel with graph capture, behind the --startup-weight-load-mode overlap flag. The tensor-parallel LMHead replaces an allgather plus scatter with a single all-to-all under pure data-parallel attention, which drops that step from 320 to 169 microseconds on a DeepSeek-V4-Pro B200 decode and moves time-per-output-token from 36.97 to 35.67 milliseconds. Non-fused allreduce sites reuse the FlashInfer MNNVL workspace rather than falling back to NCCL.
explainer.whyItMatters: Restart time is a real operational cost for anyone running large open models: autoscaling, rolling upgrades and crash recovery all pay it, and 85 seconds per replica adds up across a fleet. Halving it makes a serving pool cheaper to move around. The microsecond-level decode savings matter less per request but compound at high throughput, and SGLang is one of the two engines most self-hosted open-weight deployments sit on.
explainer.forWho: inference and platform engineers self-hosting open models

items.title: Bot Preference Sync — Cloudflare writes your robots.txt to match your bot rules
items.summary: Bot Preference Sync generates and updates your robots.txt from the AI bot policy you set in the Cloudflare dashboard, so the published file and the rules enforced at the edge stay the same. Free through Enterprise.

quickFacts.label: Search / Agent options
quickFacts.value: Allow, block on ad pages, or block everywhere

faq.q: Does Bot Preference Sync overwrite an existing robots.txt?
faq.a: No. Cloudflare states that if a site owner already has a robots.txt file, the content Bot Preference Sync adds is prepended to the existing material, so any Disallow directives already in the file are kept. The generated block sits between a BEGIN Cloudflare Bot Preference Sync marker and a matching END marker, leaving the rest of the file untouched.

faq.q: How much does Bot Preference Sync cost?
faq.a: Bot Preference Sync costs nothing extra. Cloudflare says the feature is available to all customers from the Free tier to Enterprise. It is on by default for new customers, and no crawler is blocked until the site owner picks a policy for the Search, Agent or Training categories in the dashboard.

faq.q: Can I block AI training but still let search engines index the site?
faq.a: Yes. Setting Training to Disallow writes a no-training preference into robots.txt. Cloudflare explains that cooperating mixed-use crawlers which take the extra Transparency step can still reach the content for search indexing, so a publisher can refuse training use without disappearing from search results.

faq.q: What happens to sites already using Cloudflare's older managed robots.txt?
faq.a: Existing users of the legacy managed robots.txt feature are not switched over silently. Cloudflare says it will prompt those customers to review and confirm their preferences in order to transition to Bot Preference Sync when it launches, so the current file is not rewritten until the owner approves the new settings.

explainer.tagline: Cloudflare builds your robots.txt out of the AI bot policy you already set in its dashboard.
explainer.whatIsIt: Bot Preference Sync writes your robots.txt for you, based on the AI bot policy you pick in the Cloudflare dashboard. Cloudflare sorts AI crawlers by the job they are doing — Search, Agent or Training — and turns your choice for each into user-agent rules in the file. It is generally available on every plan, from Free to Enterprise.
explainer.howItWorks: The generated rules are prepended to any robots.txt you already have, wrapped in BEGIN and END marker comments, so your own Disallow lines survive untouched. Bot names inside that block come from BotBase, Cloudflare's database of tracked crawlers, and are refreshed periodically as crawlers appear or change their user-agent. Search and Agent each take one of three settings; Training is a simple Allow or Disallow.
explainer.whyItMatters: A hand-maintained robots.txt drifts away from what a site actually enforces at the edge, and crawler operators read the file rather than the firewall. Cloudflare's stated goal is that 'what you say to the world and what you enforce at the edge are kept in sync.' For publishers, the Training setting also puts a no-training preference in writing without costing them search traffic.
explainer.forWho: publishers and site owners
explainer.tryIt: Set your Search, Agent and Training preferences in Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control dashboard.

items.title: OpenRouter Image Benchmarks — 39 image models on one page of hard prompts
items.summary: OpenRouter Image Benchmarks runs the same set of deliberately hard prompts through every image model it hosts and shows the raw pictures side by side, sortable by cost or generation time. Free to view, no account needed.

explainer.tagline: Every image model OpenRouter hosts, run through the same hard prompts, with the raw outputs shown in one grid.
explainer.whatIsIt: Image Benchmarks is a free public page from OpenRouter that puts the same deliberately hard prompts through every image model on the platform and shows the actual pictures in a grid. The announcement counts 39 image models. You judge the outputs with your own eyes instead of reading a single score.
explainer.howItWorks: Prompts are grouped into seven challenge families — improbable scenes, counting, text, spatial relations, negation, editing and consistency — each aimed at a known weak spot, with named tests such as Full Wine Glass, Three Fingers, Long Exact String, Occlusion, Minimal Diff and Four References. OpenRouter notes that 'LLM-as-a-judge evals can't yet capture the details a human would notice,' which is why the page shows raw output rather than a graded number.
explainer.whyItMatters: OpenRouter opens by saying that next to the many LLM benchmarks, 'picking an image model can feel arbitrary.' The grid sorts by cost or by time, and the listed models span roughly $0.006 to $0.25 per image and 3.6 to 208.2 seconds per generation, so a team can see what the cheap and slow ends of that range actually produce before committing.

items.title: Simon Willison — Linus Torvalds let an AI write a Linux kernel commit message
items.summary: Linus Torvalds credited an AI with much of the grunt work behind an Intel Xe driver fix, and let the AI write the commit message. Simon Willison quotes it: 24 debug patches and 18 kernel boots to find a one-line bug.

explainer.tagline: Linus Torvalds called it a debug session from hell, and gave an AI credit for doing most of the grunt work.
explainer.whatIsIt: A Linux kernel commit from Linus Torvalds now credits an AI, and Simon Willison's post collects the quote. The commit fixes the Intel Xe graphics driver so it stops handing out flat CCS storage as usable VRAM, which was letting the compression hardware overwrite kernel allocations and crash the desktop compositor on a Battlemage G21 card. Torvalds called it "a debug session from hell, enormously helped by an AI doing much of the grunt-work", and said he let the AI write the commit message itself.
explainer.howItWorks: The actual fix is one line: a round_up() that should have been a round_down() when working out the flat CCS offset. Getting there took 24 patches that added more and more debug output and 18 kernel boots, per the commit message. Torvalds notes the AI repeatedly stated the problem was impossible and unsolvable and suggested just writing a report about it, but kept adding debug code and analysing the results faithfully when he pushed back.
explainer.whyItMatters: An AI credited inside a commit by the Linux kernel's creator is a concrete signal about where these tools help right now: not finding the bug, but grinding through debug output without getting bored. The account also names the failure mode engineers keep hitting — the model calls a problem unsolvable and wants to stop, and only reaches the answer because a stubborn human refuses to accept that.

items.title: LLM 0.33 — Simon Willison's CLI moves to the OpenAI Python 3.x library
items.summary: Simon Willison releases LLM 0.33, an update to his Python CLI for language models. The release moves onto the OpenAI Python library 3.x and httpx2, lets embedding commands take a per-call API key, and allows templates to be combined.

explainer.tagline: LLM 0.33 rebases Simon Willison's model CLI on the OpenAI Python 3.x library and adds per-call embedding keys.
explainer.whatIsIt: LLM 0.33 moves Simon Willison's command-line tool for language models onto the OpenAI Python library 3.x and swaps its HTTP client from httpx to httpx2. The release also lets `llm embed` and `llm embed-multi` accept a `--key` flag, shows the output of server-side tool calls inside `llm logs`, and lets `-t/--template` be repeated so one template supplies the model settings while another supplies the prompt.
explainer.howItWorks: The per-call key travels through a new `key=` argument on `EmbeddingModel.embed()`, `embed_multi()` and the matching `Collection` methods, so a plugin receives the resolved key without the shared model state changing; plugins that still read `self.key` keep working through a compatibility fallback. Server-side tool output is stored with a `server_executed` marker, which is how `llm logs --json` and `llm logs --short` tell it apart from tools that ran on the local machine.
explainer.whyItMatters: Plugin authors feel this release first: the jump to OpenAI 3.x and httpx2 raises the dependency floor for every plugin in the LLM ecosystem, and the `--key` argument removes a long-standing reason to mutate shared model state just to embed with a second account. For everyday users, repeated `-t` flags mean a saved model configuration and a saved prompt no longer have to live in the same template file.
explainer.forWho: Python developers and LLM plugin authors

items.title: Rafal Cymerys — AI-written docs now get skipped before they get read
items.summary: Rafal Cymerys writes that he now skips work documents that look AI-written, the same way people ignore banner ads. He lists the tells: Claude-style phrasing, routine features sold as breakthroughs, and long text that says little.

explainer.tagline: Rafal Cymerys says constant exposure to AI-written text has trained him to stop reading it at all.
explainer.whatIsIt: 'I'm becoming AI-blind' is an essay by Rafal Cymerys, CTO of the AI consultancy Upside, about a reflex he did not choose. Cymerys writes that his eyes now slide off any work document carrying the marks of AI generation, before he has decided whether it is worth reading. He treats this as pattern recognition rather than snobbery — people really can spot low-effort machine text.
explainer.howItWorks: The tells listed in the essay are specific. Cymerys names Claude-style phrasing such as 'This cuts just through it', verbose internal reasoning left sitting in the text, and routine work sold as a breakthrough — his example is a document that dramatizes 'the checkboxes in an RBAC configuration view'. A fourth tell is tonal mismatch: sensible strategy stitched to technical jargon that means nothing.
explainer.whyItMatters: Banner blindness is the comparison Cymerys reaches for: heavy exposure trains the brain to filter out a whole format, and he argues the same thing has now happened to AI prose. The cost is that useful documents get thrown out with the noise — 'the same AI that was supposed to make me more productive, is what's now slowing me down.' The essay drew 424 points and 429 comments on Hacker News.

items.title: Thomas Ptacek — coding agents make native apps cheap, so stop building TUIs
items.summary: Thomas Ptacek argues that terminal UIs only ever existed because of modems and because Unix developers avoided GUI toolkits. Coding agents now write idiomatic SwiftUI, so a small native Mac app costs about as little as a CLI.

explainer.tagline: Thomas Ptacek says coding agents removed the last excuse for shipping a terminal UI instead of a real app.
explainer.whatIsIt: 'Stop Making TUIs' is an essay by Thomas Ptacek arguing that developers should stop building terminal user interfaces and build native graphical apps instead. Ptacek's claim about why TUIs exist is blunt: 'TUIs exist for just two reasons: modems, and because Unix nerds didn't want to learn Motif.' Both reasons, he writes, expired a long time ago.
explainer.howItWorks: The evidence is a run of small macOS apps Ptacek built with Claude and Codex agents: MDV.app, a Markdown viewer; DJ Roomba, an Apple Music player with an LLM agent inside; Self Driving Wiki.app, a wiki backed by SQLite; a SageMath calculator front end; a menu-bar thermometer called Thermite; and an Apple TV remote. He never opened Xcode — the build is a plain Makefile — and pointed the agents at skills for macOS design, Paul Hudson's SwiftUI material, and Airbnb's Swift style guide.
explainer.whyItMatters: Native interface work used to need a specialist, which is the real reason backend developers kept shipping command-line tools. That boundary is what Ptacek says agents dissolved: an agent follows Apple's own SwiftUI patterns closely enough to produce something reasonable, so the cheap default for a personal tool moves from the terminal to the desktop. Simon Willison, linking the piece the next day, said he is 'running out of excuses'.
explainer.forWho: backend and systems developers
explainer.tryIt: Pick one throwaway CLI and ask a coding agent to rebuild it as a native app.

items.title: OpenAI regional processing — pick an inference region per API request
items.summary: OpenAI now lets a single API call choose where it runs. Swap api.openai.com for a regional domain such as eu.api.openai.com or jp.api.openai.com and that request is processed in that region. Ten regions are live.

quickFacts.label: What's new
quickFacts.value: Region chosen per request, not per project

quickFacts.label: Regions
quickFacts.value: US, EU, UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, India, Singapore, South Korea, UAE

quickFacts.label: Requirement
quickFacts.value: API key from a project with Global geography

quickFacts.label: Extra approval
quickFacts.value: Non-US regions need abuse-monitoring approval and a Modified Retention amendment

faq.q: Do I need a separate OpenAI project or API key for each region?
faq.a: No. Regional processing works from one API key belonging to a project with Global geography, which is the point of the change. OpenAI's Python example reuses a single client and a single key, overriding only the base URL per call, so a region no longer implies a separate project, key rotation or quota to manage.

faq.q: What approvals does OpenAI require before a non-US region can be used?
faq.a: OpenAI keeps its existing eligibility rules in place for regional processing. For any non-US region a customer must obtain approval for abuse monitoring controls and execute a Modified Retention amendment. The UAE region carries a further requirement: it needs its own separate approval on top of that, so access is not automatic.

faq.q: Does every OpenAI model and endpoint support regional processing?
faq.a: No. Only the endpoints and model snapshots explicitly marked as supporting regional processing in OpenAI's documentation tables accept a regional domain. The listed routes include /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses and /v1/embeddings, and the supported model snapshots differ by region, so the tables have to be checked per region.

faq.q: Can global and regional requests live in the same application?
faq.a: Yes. Because regional processing at OpenAI is selected by hostname, one application can send some traffic to api.openai.com and route other traffic to a regional domain, using the same key. OpenAI's SDK example shows exactly this pattern: keep one client, change base_url on the calls that need a fixed region.

explainer.tagline: One API key, ten regional domains — choose where each OpenAI request is processed.
explainer.whatIsIt: Regional processing is now a per-request choice at OpenAI instead of a per-project setting. An API key from a project with Global geography can call a region-prefixed domain — eu.api.openai.com, jp.api.openai.com and eight others — and that one request is handled in the chosen region. OpenAI shipped it in the API changelog on 21 August 2026 and documented it in the data controls guide.
explainer.howItWorks: The routing decision rides entirely on the hostname. The request path, body and API key stay the same, so client code only changes its base URL; OpenAI's Python SDK example reuses one client and overrides base_url per call. Eligibility and data-retention rules are unchanged, and a regional domain is only accepted by the endpoints and model snapshots the docs mark as supported.
explainer.whyItMatters: Teams under data-residency rules previously had to split traffic across separate region-locked OpenAI projects, each with its own key, quota and deployment. Choosing the region at call time lets one codebase serve an EU customer and a US customer from the same key, which turns residency into a routing decision instead of a fork of the stack.
explainer.forWho: enterprise and compliance-bound API teams

image.alt: OpenAI API documentation card for data controls and regional processing

items.title: Benchmark Fitting — Hugging Face scores how much ASR models memorize tests
items.summary: Hugging Face and Hume AI added a Benchmark Fitting tab to the Open ASR Leaderboard. Three probes check whether a speech model transcribes the audio or repeats the reference. Six of 11 models dropped audible words the reference lacked.

quickFacts.label: Maker
quickFacts.value: Hugging Face with Hume AI, Artificial Analysis and Treble Technologies

quickFacts.label: What's new
quickFacts.value: Benchmark Fitting tab on the Open ASR Leaderboard

quickFacts.label: Probes
quickFacts.value: Reference disagreement, masked entity retrieval, orthographic switching

quickFacts.label: Models tested
quickFacts.value: 11, including Whisper large-v3, Parakeet, Canary, Qwen3-ASR and Voxtral

quickFacts.label: Also launched
quickFacts.value: Real World VoiceEQ and a far-field ASR leaderboard

quickFacts.label: Paper
quickFacts.value: Towards Quantifying Benchmark Optimization in ASR Models

faq.q: Does a low word error rate still mean an ASR model is accurate?
faq.a: Not on its own, according to the Benchmark Fitting analysis. Hugging Face and Hume AI report that the highest-scoring models were the most likely to reproduce erroneous VoxPopuli transcripts, so part of a strong word error rate reflects learned test-set patterns. The new tab is meant to be read next to word error rate, not instead of it.

faq.q: Are the ASR test sets themselves clean?
faq.a: Not fully. The Benchmark Fitting team found that 40% of VoxPopuli test clips contain potential reference errors, touching about 3% of all reference words. Artificial Analysis published a cleaned version as VoxPopuli-Cleaned-AA, and the reference-disagreement probe uses those known errors to measure how often a model repeats them.

faq.q: Did the models behave differently on freshly recorded audio?
faq.a: Yes, and that is the control the study leans on. The Benchmark Fitting write-up reports weaker benchmark-optimization behaviour on newly collected audio from the same domains — European Parliament and LibriVox recordings made in 2026 — which separates genuine domain skill from memorization of the published test sets.

faq.q: How can the Benchmark Fitting results be reproduced?
faq.a: The evaluation scripts sit under benchmark_fitting in the Apache-2.0 huggingface/open_asr_leaderboard repository, and Hume AI published its own code at HumeAI/asr-benchmark-optimization. Hugging Face also released the un-normalized model outputs in a public bucket, so the scoring can be rechecked without re-running all eleven speech models.

explainer.tagline: A new leaderboard tab measures how much a speech model memorized the test set instead of hearing the audio.
explainer.whatIsIt: The Open ASR Leaderboard now carries a Benchmark Fitting tab, built by Hugging Face with Hume AI, Artificial Analysis and Treble Technologies. Per model, it reports how much of a good word error rate comes from learned test-set patterns rather than transcription skill. Two further boards launched alongside it: Real World VoiceEQ and a far-field ASR leaderboard.
explainer.howItWorks: Three behavioural probes drive the score. Reference disagreement checks whether a model repeats a known transcript error instead of the words actually spoken. Masked entity retrieval silences a number in the audio and sees whether the model fills it back in — some models did so 30–40% of the time on LibriSpeech. Orthographic switching tests whether a model copies each dataset's house style, matching conventions such as "Mr." against "Mister" up to 90% of the time.
explainer.whyItMatters: Word error rate is how most teams pick a speech vendor, and these results argue that leading scores are partly a test-taking skill: six of eleven models dropped audible phrases when the audio contradicted the benchmark reference. Anyone comparing ASR systems now has a second column that estimates how much of the headline number survives contact with their own recordings.
explainer.forWho: speech ML engineers and teams choosing an ASR vendor

image.alt: Thumbnail for the Hugging Face post on measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

items.title: NoBuzz — a Claude Code skill that rewrites Claude's replies in plain English
items.summary: NoBuzz is a Claude Code skill, /debuzz, that sends Claude's last reply to the Antigravity CLI and prints back a plain-English version. Three modes — colleague, manager and director — set how much detail survives.

explainer.tagline: NoBuzz hands Claude's answer to a second model and prints the plain-English rewrite instead.
explainer.whatIsIt: NoBuzz adds a /debuzz command to Claude Code that translates Claude's last reply into plain English. The skill ships three modes: colleague keeps every file path and code block intact, manager gives what happened, why it matters and what's next at about a third the length with no code, and director returns three to five sentences covering outcome, impact and ask. The repo is MIT-licensed and went up on GitHub on 21 August 2026.
explainer.howItWorks: The mechanism is a shell-out, not a prompt tweak. The skill writes the previous answer to a temporary file, then calls the Antigravity CLI (agy) with plain-English style instructions. Because agy's headless mode does not read stdin and will not open files outside the project, the text goes straight into the prompt. Claude prints the returned rewrite verbatim and is not allowed to edit it, so the original voice cannot creep back in. When agy fails — usually an auth problem — Claude offers its own rewrite with a clear label.
explainer.whyItMatters: Style complaints about coding agents usually end in a longer system prompt that the model drifts away from within a few turns. Routing the answer through a separate tool makes the rewrite a fixed step instead of a request. The Hacker News thread, posted under the title 'Claudette', reached 212 points and 150 comments. The trade-off is setup: NoBuzz needs both Claude Code and the Antigravity CLI installed and signed in, so it is a two-vendor tool.

items.title: Codex CLI 0.149.0 — a dashboard for every running agent task
items.summary: Codex CLI 0.149.0 adds an interactive `codex agents` dashboard for searching, starting, opening, renaming and stopping tasks. The same build adds `codex queue`, which sends a message into an existing local or remote session.

explainer.tagline: Codex CLI 0.149.0 puts every agent task behind one searchable dashboard you can drive with shortcuts.
explainer.whatIsIt: An interactive `codex agents` dashboard is the headline change in Codex CLI 0.149.0. It searches, starts, opens, renames and stops tasks from one screen, with configurable shortcuts. A second new command, `codex queue`, sends a message into a session that is already running, local or remote. Codex CLI itself is OpenAI's terminal coding agent, written in Rust and shared under Apache-2.0.
explainer.howItWorks: Working-directory control moves inside the terminal UI: `/cd`, `/pwd` and `/cwd` set and report where a session runs, so you no longer restart Codex CLI to change folders. Vim editing picks up character replacement and more change motions such as `cw`, `c$` and `cc`. The `codex doctor` check now diagnoses endpoint protection, network and proxy failures, desktop app state, and update connectivity.
explainer.whyItMatters: Running several coding agents at once used to mean guessing which terminal held which task. The dashboard and the queue command give that fleet a single front door. A quieter fix matters just as much for safety: resumed and forked threads now restore the permission profile they were started with, instead of silently falling back to whatever the current defaults happen to be. SDK users also gain exact CLI config overrides and can pick `max` or `ultra` reasoning effort.
explainer.forWho: developers running several Codex tasks in parallel

faq.q: Is Codex CLI open source?
faq.a: Yes. Codex CLI is published under the Apache-2.0 license on GitHub at openai/codex, where it has 111,133 stars. The agent is written in Rust and described by OpenAI as a lightweight coding agent that runs in your terminal. The npm package @openai/codex ships the same 0.149.0 build and needs Node.js 16 or higher.

faq.q: Can I send pull requests to the Codex repository?
faq.a: OpenAI would rather you did not open one cold. The 0.149.0 documentation update clarifies that external contributions to Codex should go through issues and design discussion rather than pull requests. The same docs pass also writes up DNS exfiltration risks and the trust limits of secure devcontainers, so start a conversation in an issue first.

faq.q: What did Codex CLI 0.149.0 fix for sub-agents?
faq.a: Codex CLI 0.149.0 removes duplicate sub-agent activity from the display and tightens terminal-UI routing for sub-agent notifications and approvals, so a prompt lands where you can answer it. Realtime WebRTC sideband connections also reconnect after an unexpected transport loss without dropping output that was still pending.

faq.q: Are there Windows-specific improvements in this Codex release?
faq.a: Yes. In Codex CLI 0.149.0, inline terminal-UI history stays available in Windows Terminal scrollback, so earlier turns do not vanish when you scroll back. The release also bounds replay buffers for inactive threads, which stops Codex from holding on to large amounts of streamed output you are no longer looking at.

faq.q: What happens to messages queued while a Codex session is idle?
faq.a: Queued messages now wake idle Codex sessions reliably in 0.149.0, rather than sitting until you touch the session yourself. The same fix resolves duplicate session names more usefully and preserves the semantics of pasted or deferred commands, so a message you queued behaves the same way it would have if you had typed it live.

items.title: NVIDIA AVO — an agent system scores 100% on ARC-AGI-3's public set
items.summary: NVIDIA AVO scored 100.00 RHAE on the 25-environment public set of ARC-AGI-3, clearing all 183 levels in 6,624 actions. Claude Opus 5 on its own scores about 30% on the same set. The private competition sets were not tested.

quickFacts.label: Base model
quickFacts.value: Claude Opus 5, with tests on GPT-5.6 Sol

quickFacts.label: GPU kernel result
quickFacts.value: Up to 3.5% over cuDNN, 10.5% over FlashAttention-4

quickFacts.label: Availability
quickFacts.value: Research paper only — no code or weights released

explainer.tagline: NVIDIA's AVO agent cleared every public ARC-AGI-3 environment, a benchmark where the best single model sat near 30%.
explainer.whatIsIt: NVIDIA AVO — short for Agentic Variation Operators — cleared all 25 environments of the ARC-AGI-3 public set with a 100.00 RHAE score. ARC-AGI-3 drops an agent into an unfamiliar turn-based world with no instructions, so it has to work out the goal and the rules by playing. NVIDIA says the run used Claude Opus 5 as the underlying model, with extra testing on GPT-5.6 Sol.
explainer.howItWorks: The design replaces the fixed mutation and crossover steps of classic evolutionary search with a coding agent that decides what to try next. Persistent memory carries earlier implementations, evaluation results, compiler and profiler output forward, so the agent resumes work instead of rebuilding its context each round. A separate supervisor watches the wider search for stalling or repeated dead ends and can redirect the main agent to another strategy.
explainer.whyItMatters: Long-horizon autonomy is the weak spot in today's agents, and this result points at the harness around a model mattering as much as the model itself. NVIDIA also ran AVO for seven straight days on GPU kernel work for multi-head attention, where it explored more than 500 optimization directions and committed 40 kernel versions. Teams building agents get a concrete design to copy: memory, a supervisor, grounded feedback and recovery.
explainer.forWho: agent researchers and systems engineers

image.alt: Abstract agentic AI graphic from NVIDIA's AVO announcement

faq.q: Is NVIDIA AVO available to download or use?
faq.a: NVIDIA has not released code, weights or an API for AVO. The developer blog points only to the research paper, 'AVO: Agentic Variation Operators for Autonomous Evolutionary Search', on arXiv. Teams who want the approach get the paper's description of the agent loop, persistent memory and supervisor, but there is no NVIDIA implementation to run today.

faq.q: Does the 100% score cover all of ARC-AGI-3?
faq.a: No. NVIDIA states the AVO results cover the 25-environment ARC-AGI-3 public set using the official scorecard and RHAE metric, and are not results on the semi-private or fully private competition sets. ARC Prize keeps those held-out sets to guard against overfitting, so the 100.00 RHAE figure is a public-set number only.

faq.q: How does AVO compare with Claude Opus 5 on its own?
faq.a: Claude Opus 5 by itself reaches roughly 30% on the ARC-AGI-3 public set, while AVO reaches 100.00 RHAE using the same model family. NVIDIA cautions that its run used a different reasoning setting and a substantially different agent system, and says the comparison should not be read as a controlled ablation.

faq.q: What does the RHAE score in ARC-AGI-3 measure?
faq.a: RHAE stands for Relative Human Action Efficiency. The ARC-AGI-3 metric combines task completion with per-level action efficiency measured against first-time human baselines, then aggregates across levels and environments. AVO used 6,624 environment actions to finish 183 levels, about 12% fewer than the 7,542 actions reported for VISTA.

faq.q: What else did NVIDIA test AVO on besides the benchmark?
faq.a: NVIDIA ran AVO on GPU kernel optimization for multi-head attention on DGX B200 systems, operating continuously for seven days. AVO explored more than 500 optimization directions and produced 40 committed kernel versions, ending with kernels that outperform cuDNN by up to 3.5% and FlashAttention-4 by up to 10.5% across the evaluated configurations.

items.title: 4DAnyone — turn one handheld video of a person into a 4D model
items.summary: 4DAnyone rebuilds a moving person in 4D from a single ordinary video. The Ant Research system generates multiview-consistent video first, then lifts it into 4D Gaussian Splatting. Code and checkpoints are public.

explainer.tagline: 4DAnyone reconstructs a moving person in 4D from one casual monocular video, with code and checkpoints released.
explainer.whatIsIt: 4DAnyone takes a casual single-camera video of a person and rebuilds them as a 4D Gaussian Splatting scene you can view from any angle over time. The work comes from Ant Research with Zhejiang University and HKUST, and was accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026. Code, checkpoints and example videos are already public.
explainer.howItWorks: The pipeline generates multiview-consistent video of the subject, then lifts those views into 4D Gaussian Splatting. Two ideas keep generation stable as the number of target views grows: Reference Context Packing compresses the reference views into a fixed-length mixed-resolution context, and Target Context Routing rotates which views are denoised together so information crosses groups. Depth-buffered skeleton renderings supply 3D-aware pose conditioning, and training adds MVGameHuman, a game-engine dataset the team built.
explainer.whyItMatters: Capturing a person in 4D normally needs a camera rig or a studio. Working from a phone-style clip puts free-viewpoint replay, avatar creation and 3D video editing in reach of people with no capture hardware. The released repo and checkpoints let researchers reproduce the result instead of only reading about it.
explainer.forWho: graphics and computer vision researchers

image.alt: 4DAnyone project card showing 4D human reconstruction from a monocular video

items.title: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp — an experimental V4 model that reads images
items.summary: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is an experimental multimodal model on the DeepSeek API that takes images alongside text. It scores 83.9 on Terminal Bench 2.1 and matches DeepSeek V4-Flash on text-only work.

explainer.tagline: An experimental DeepSeek model that adds image understanding to the V4-Flash line, at V4-Flash prices.
explainer.whatIsIt: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp adds image input to DeepSeek's V4-Flash line. The model takes mixed text-and-image prompts through the Chat Completions, Messages and Responses APIs, so an agent can read a screenshot, a chart or a photo in the same call it reads text. DeepSeek labels the model experimental and ships it under the id deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp.
explainer.howItWorks: Images are turned into tokens and billed like text, and can be passed as base64 data, as an external URL, or through the DeepSeek Files API. On pure-text work — agents, reasoning, world knowledge — DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp performs on par with the official DeepSeek V4-Flash, so sight is added without a text-quality trade-off. DeepSeek Harness 0.1.1 shipped the same day with out-of-the-box support for the new model.
explainer.whyItMatters: Agent benchmarks that need visual understanding are where DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp gains the most. DeepSeek says the jump over DeepSeek V4-Flash is significant and brings its multimodal agent skills close to Opus-4.8, at flash-tier prices. Teams building screen-reading, chart-parsing or document agents get a much cheaper model to test against.
explainer.forWho: developers building vision-capable AI agents

faq.q: How much does DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp cost?
faq.a: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is billed at DeepSeek V4-Flash rates. Off-peak, input is $0.22 per million tokens on a cache miss and $0.007 on a cache hit, and output is $0.66 per million tokens. Peak rates are double the off-peak rates, and DeepSeek sets peak hours at 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC.

faq.q: Is DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp stable enough for production?
faq.a: DeepSeek labels V4-Flash-Vision-Exp an experimental model and gives it an -exp suffix in its id, so treat it as a preview rather than a settled endpoint. Because its text performance matches the official DeepSeek V4-Flash, a team can trial vision calls on the experimental id while keeping text traffic on the stable V4-Flash model.

faq.q: How does DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp compare to DeepSeek V4-Flash?
faq.a: On pure-text work — agents, reasoning and world knowledge — DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp performs on par with the official DeepSeek V4-Flash. The gap shows on agent benchmarks that need visual understanding, where DeepSeek says V4-Flash-Vision-Exp makes a significant leap over V4-Flash and comes close to Opus-4.8. Price and the 1M-token context window are the same.

faq.q: Which benchmark scores did DeepSeek publish for V4-Flash-Vision-Exp?
faq.a: DeepSeek listed nine results for V4-Flash-Vision-Exp in its change log: Terminal Bench 2.1 at 83.9, NL2Repo at 57.7, DeepSWE at 59.3, DSBench-Hard at 63.6, AutomationBench (public) at 25.7, ApexBench pass@1 at 36.5, Agents' Last Exam at 27.3, Chartography at 64.3, and ZeroBench pass@5 at 35.0.

items.title: GLM-5.3-Flash — Z.ai opens the weights of the model that was Ox Alpha
items.summary: GLM-5.3-Flash is the open-weights release of the stealth model that topped OpenRouter as Ox Alpha. Z.ai calls it the first natively multimodal GLM-5 model: 320B total parameters, 18B active, MIT licensed, with a 1M-token context.

explainer.tagline: The stealth model that topped OpenRouter now has a name, a model card and MIT-licensed weights: GLM-5.3-Flash.
explainer.whatIsIt: GLM-5.3-Flash is a 320B-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only 18B parameters per token, and Z.ai calls it the first natively multimodal model in the GLM-5 series — it reads images as well as text. It is the model that ran on OpenRouter for a week under the anonymous name Ox Alpha, where it reached the top of the usage leaderboard with more than double DeepSeek's traffic. Z.ai published the blog post, the model card and the API documentation on August 26, 2026.
explainer.howItWorks: A hybrid attention design mixes sparse and linear attention, which is how Z.ai keeps cost down at a 1M-token context. Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections are used to improve scaling efficiency, and pretraining ran on a 30T-token multimodal corpus. Native multimodal visual coding lets the model look at an interface or a rendered result and act on what it sees, rather than working from text descriptions of the screen.
explainer.whyItMatters: MIT-licensed weights mean a team can self-host the same model it was testing for free on OpenRouter, which is the difference between trialling a 1M-token context and building on it. Z.ai says GLM-5.3-Flash beats GLM-5.2 across benchmarks and real workloads at one-tenth the price, and approaches Claude Opus 4.8 on coding and agentic benchmarks. The weights run under SGLang, vLLM, TokenSpeed and KTransformers.
explainer.forWho: teams running long-context coding and agent workloads
explainer.tryIt: Model: zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash on Hugging Face; API model ID glm-5.3-flash

faq.q: Is GLM-5.3-Flash the same model as Ox Alpha?
faq.a: Yes. Ox Alpha was the anonymous name GLM-5.3-Flash ran under on OpenRouter, listed by a provider called Stealth with no lab attached. Z.ai confirmed to Bloomberg News on August 26, 2026 that the model was a new GLM-series release and that the weights would follow, then published GLM-5.3-Flash the same day with a blog post and a Hugging Face model card.

faq.q: How does GLM-5.3-Flash compare with GLM-5.3?
faq.a: GLM-5.3, released on August 14, 2026, is text-only and reuses the GLM-5.2 base model. GLM-5.3-Flash is a separate 320B mixture-of-experts model that reads images as well as text, activates 18B parameters per token, and is built on a hybrid sparse and linear attention design. Z.ai's documentation gives GLM-5.3-Flash three times the quota of GLM-5.3.

faq.q: What hardware or serving stack does GLM-5.3-Flash need?
faq.a: Z.ai lists four supported local deployment paths for GLM-5.3-Flash: SGLang, vLLM, TokenSpeed and KTransformers, each with its own cookbook or recipe. Only 18B of the 320B parameters are active per token, so serving cost tracks the active count rather than the full weight size, but the whole checkpoint still has to be held or offloaded somewhere.

faq.q: Can I use GLM-5.3-Flash without downloading the weights?
faq.a: Yes. GLM-5.3-Flash is served through the Z.ai API platform under the model ID glm-5.3-flash, documented at docs.z.ai, and it also ran on OpenRouter during its free stealth week as Ox Alpha. Z.ai's API guide describes a points-based quota rather than a flat per-token rate, and it grants three times the quota available for GLM-5.3.

image.alt: Hugging Face model card banner for zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash

items.title: SWE-bench Science — the best coding agent fixes under half of 119 science bugs
items.summary: SWE-bench Science is an MIT-licensed benchmark of 119 repository-level tasks drawn from 98 scientific codebases across 20 domains. On the published leaderboard, Claude Opus 5 leads with 47.90% Pass@1.

explainer.tagline: 119 real bug-fixing tasks pulled from 98 scientific codebases, where every agent tested fails more than half.
explainer.whatIsIt: SWE-bench Science tests coding agents on software that scientists actually run: 119 repository-level tasks across 98 GitHub repositories and 20 scientific domains, covering density-functional theory, plasma stability, genomics, molecular dynamics and computational physics. Python dominates, with C++, MATLAB/Octave and Fortran also present. OpenMOSS released the dataset on Hugging Face under MIT.
explainer.howItWorks: Tasks are split into three paradigms — Issue-driven, Expert-exploratory and Engineering-integration — and Pass@1 is reported for each as well as overall. Every task ships Docker container specs for both environment setup and verification, plus the repository URL, commit hash and source license, so a fix only counts when the scientific result checks out.
explainer.whyItMatters: The leaderboard puts Claude Opus 5 (max) first at 47.90% Pass@1, GPT-5.6 Sol (max) at 46.22% and DeepSeek V4 Pro (max) at 42.02%, so more than half of these bugs go unfixed by every agent tested. The paper names four repeat failures: knowledge gaps, surface-level repairs, incomplete integration and poor generalization. An ablation found that scientific guidance helps only when it is well aligned, and hurts when it is not.
explainer.forWho: researchers pointing coding agents at scientific code
explainer.tryIt: Load OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science from the Hugging Face datasets hub

items.title: Claude Code 2.1.238 — plugin marketplaces can mint their own auth headers
items.summary: Claude Code 2.1.238 adds headersHelper, a command that mints HTTP headers such as a short-lived token for private plugin marketplaces. The same build fixes unbounded memory growth in long interactive sessions.

explainer.tagline: Private plugin marketplaces can now hand Claude Code a fresh token for every catalog fetch.
explainer.whatIsIt: Claude Code 2.1.238 adds headersHelper to plugin marketplaces: a command that mints HTTP headers, such as a short-lived token, for catalog and same-origin archive fetches. A catalog entry's helper runs only when you install or update that plugin, after Claude Code prints the command it will run and asks [y/N]. That closes the gap for teams whose internal plugin registry sits behind short-lived credentials.
explainer.howItWorks: Self-hosted runners get two new flags in the same build. The --defer-shutdown-max-min option keeps serving attached sessions after SIGTERM for a set number of minutes, parks whatever is left, then exits. The --proxy-authorization-command and --proxy-authorization-file options supply a freshly issued Proxy-Authorization header on every connection, for egress proxies that demand one.
explainer.whyItMatters: Anyone who leaves the terminal agent open all day gets the bigger win: unbounded memory growth in long interactive sessions is fixed, because subagent tool results are now released once they leave the recent display window. The 2.1.237 build from the same day added a built-in "Concise" output style that skips preamble and narration.
explainer.forWho: teams running private plugins or self-hosted runners

quickFacts.label: Notable fix
quickFacts.value: Memory growth in long interactive sessions

faq.q: Which Claude Code versions shipped in this cycle?
faq.a: Claude Code put out five builds between August 17 and August 20, 2026: 2.1.234 on the 17th, 2.1.235 on the 18th, 2.1.236 on the 19th, and both 2.1.237 and 2.1.238 on the 20th. Version 2.1.238 is the newest entry in the changelog, and it carries the plugin-marketplace and self-hosted-runner changes.

faq.q: Do I have to approve a plugin marketplace's headersHelper before it runs?
faq.a: Yes. Claude Code shows the headersHelper command first, then claude plugin install and claude plugin update ask [y/N] before running it, unless you pass -y. A helper defined in a project .mcp.json, a plugin, or an agent file also runs without inherited credential environment variables, so it cannot quietly pick up your secrets.

faq.q: Does the new Concise output style make Claude Code less thorough?
faq.a: No. The Claude Code changelog for 2.1.237 states that the Concise style leads with results and skips preamble and narration while doing the work just as thoroughly. It changes how much Claude Code narrates, not how much it does. You select it under Output style in /config.

faq.q: Why were long Claude Code sessions using more and more memory?
faq.a: Subagent tool results were kept in memory for the whole session. Claude Code 2.1.238 releases them once they leave the recent display window, which stops the unbounded growth. The same build also clears leftover /tmp/claude-*-cwd files when a Bash command is killed, times out, or is interrupted.

image.alt: GitHub repository card for anthropics/claude-code

items.title: EnvHarness — Google's wrapper layer makes static agent benchmarks adapt
items.summary: EnvHarness wraps an existing agent benchmark so its behaviour can be reshaped without editing the benchmark itself. The paper reports up to a 9.0-point gain on held-out tasks with 9.8% fewer steps. Code is Apache-2.0.

quickFacts.label: Also credited
quickFacts.value: Washington University in St. Louis, UNC Chapel Hill

faq.q: Is EnvHarness open source?
faq.a: Yes. EnvHarness ships as Apache-2.0 Python code at github.com/google-research/envharness, published alongside the arXiv paper on 20 August 2026. The repository sits under the google-research organisation. A project page at envharness.com hosts a browser playground, so the framework can be inspected and tried without an API key or a paid account.

faq.q: Which benchmarks did EnvHarness improve, and by how much?
faq.a: The EnvHarness paper reports three headline results. On WebArena the agent moves from 38.7 to 41.6. On SWE-bench Verified it moves from 47.7 to 52.6. On ALFWorld it moves from 61.7 to 68.3, the largest jump at 5.9 points. Across five benchmarks in four domains the best held-out gain reaches 9.0 points.

faq.q: Does EnvHarness require rewriting an existing benchmark?
faq.a: No. EnvHarness customises an environment through the standard reset() and step() interface alone, using composable wrapper components. The interface contract and the original benchmark's verifiers both stay intact, so scores remain comparable to the unmodified benchmark and maintainers do not have to fork or patch the environment's own code.

faq.q: How does EnvHarness compare to training an agent in the real environment?
faq.a: The paper includes that comparison as a separate column. Learning in real environments scores 38.5 on WebArena, 49.9 on SWE-bench Verified and 62.4 on ALFWorld. EnvHarness environments beat all three, at 41.6, 52.6 and 68.3. On WebArena, real-environment training actually scored slightly below the base agent's 38.7.

faq.q: Can I try EnvHarness without running any code?
faq.a: Yes. The EnvHarness project page at envharness.com includes a playable demo built on the 24 game, where four cards are combined with plus, minus, times and divide, two at a time, until one number is left. Visitors can edit environment components live and watch how the policy's observations diverge from the real environment state.

explainer.tagline: EnvHarness reshapes an existing agent benchmark into a training environment without touching the benchmark's own code.
explainer.whatIsIt: EnvHarness turns a fixed agent benchmark into an environment you can edit. Google Cloud AI Research built it with Washington University in St. Louis and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and released the code under Apache-2.0. A second part, EnvRigger, watches an agent's trajectories and writes new environment components aimed at the weak spots it finds.
explainer.howItWorks: Composable wrappers do the work. Customisation in EnvHarness happens through the standard reset() and step() calls alone, so the interface contract and the original benchmark's verifiers both stay intact. EnvRigger then reads agent trajectories and synthesises targeted components from them, which lets the environment and the policy keep changing together instead of the environment staying frozen.
explainer.whyItMatters: Agent training environments are hand-built and static, so they stop teaching once an agent gets good at them. The EnvHarness paper reports up to a 9.0-point gain on held-out instances with 9.8% fewer execution steps across five benchmarks in four domains. Teams that already run WebArena, SWE-bench Verified or ALFWorld can reuse those environments for training rather than building new ones.
explainer.forWho: agent and RL researchers

items.title: Waymo's custom AI chip — a 5nm ASIC that runs 1,000+ TOPS in the car
items.summary: Waymo announced its own 5nm ASIC, made by TSMC, that runs over 1,000 TOPS of machine-learning work inside its robotaxis. The chip fuses lidar, radar and 13 camera streams in real time and is in production in Waymo's latest robotaxi generation.

quickFacts.label: Redundancy
quickFacts.value: Two independent engines; one takes over on fault

quickFacts.label: Cooling
quickFacts.value: Tied into the vehicle's liquid cooling system

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: In production in Waymo's latest robotaxi generation

faq.q: Is Waymo dropping Nvidia and AMD chips?
faq.a: Waymo still lists AMD, Micron, NVIDIA, Samsung, SanDisk, Socionext and TSMC as partners in its announcement. The custom ASIC takes over the machine-learning front end, while The Register reports that parts from those suppliers still handle non-ML work such as orchestration, data movement and logging. Bloomberg reports the chip reduces Waymo's reliance on outside vendors rather than ending it.

faq.q: How does Waymo's chip compare to Nvidia's self-driving systems?
faq.a: Waymo's ASIC delivers more than 1,000 TOPS, which Bloomberg reports puts it on par with Nvidia's latest systems for autonomous driving. Bloomberg also notes that TSMC's 5nm process is no longer the foundry's most advanced node, so the gain comes from shaping the silicon around Waymo's own sensor workload rather than from a lead in manufacturing.

faq.q: What happens if the Waymo chip fails while the car is driving?
faq.a: Waymo built the compute as two independent engines that normally run full parallel workloads as one unit. Waymo says that if one engine hits a fault, the other seamlessly takes over, so the robotaxi keeps processing sensor data. The module also ties into the vehicle's liquid cooling system instead of running its own separate cooling.

faq.q: Is the Waymo chip already on the road?
faq.a: Waymo says the ASIC is in production in its latest robotaxi generation, per Bloomberg's report on the August 20, 2026 announcement. Waymo's blog post does not give a fleet-wide rollout date and does not say how many vehicles carry the chip today, so the rest of the fleet timeline stays open.

explainer.tagline: Waymo now designs the silicon that turns its robotaxi's sensor data into driving decisions.
explainer.whatIsIt: Waymo has built its own 5nm ASIC to run the machine-learning work inside its robotaxis. The chip delivers over 1,000 TOPS aimed at front-end sensor processing and neural network inference. Waymo describes it in an August 20, 2026 blog post from VP of Engineering Satish Jeyachandran and Compute Lead Daniel Rosenband. Bloomberg reports the chip is in production in Waymo's latest robotaxi generation.
explainer.howItWorks: Sensor fusion is the job. The ASIC takes lidar, radar and camera streams and turns them into one picture of the road, handling 13 high-resolution cameras at once and in real time. Waymo built the compute as two independent engines that run full parallel workloads as a single unit, and it plugs into the car's liquid cooling loop instead of sitting in a separate cooled box. The Register reports Waymo used Intel FPGAs for sensor processing before this chip.
explainer.whyItMatters: Latency is the payoff. Waymo wants to shorten the gap between light hitting a sensor and the car steering or braking, which it calls pixels-to-actuation. Owning the chip also lets Waymo shape the silicon around its own models instead of waiting on a vendor roadmap. Bloomberg reports the move cuts Waymo's reliance on outside suppliers such as Nvidia and AMD, though Waymo still names those companies among its partners.
explainer.forWho: autonomous-driving engineers, edge-AI and custom-silicon teams

items.title: Slack Code — AI coding agents get a channel the whole team can watch
items.summary: Slack Code turns a coding agent's work into a shared Slack channel with tabs for the plan, the code diffs and a live preview. Claude, Devin, GitHub Copilot and Vercel work at launch; ChatGPT is coming soon.

quickFacts.label: What it is
quickFacts.value: Shared Slack channels for AI coding agents

faq.q: Which AI coding agents work with Slack Code today?
faq.a: Slack Code is live for teams already using the Claude (Anthropic), Devin (Cognition), GitHub Copilot and Vercel integrations. Slack says ChatGPT by OpenAI is coming soon. You start a code channel by mentioning one of those agents in an existing conversation, so the agent you already use in Slack is the one that opens the channel.

faq.q: Does Slack Code cost extra?
faq.a: Slack's announcement of Slack Code does not list a price, a separate add-on, or a plan requirement, so anything about cost would be a guess. What the post does say is that Slack Code is live today for teams that already have the supported agent integrations connected to their workspace.

faq.q: Can someone approve an agent's changes before they ship?
faq.a: Yes. Slack Code routes high-stakes changes to a person for approval inside the channel, in Slack's words "right in the channel". Teammates read the same conversation the agent is working from, watch code diffs appear, view a live preview of the output, and leave feedback the agent folds into the next attempt before anything is merged.

faq.q: What happens to a code channel after the work is finished?
faq.a: A Slack Code channel archives itself when the assignment completes, so, as Slack puts it, "nothing sprawls, but everything stays searchable". The archived channel remains a searchable record of the prompt, the agent's tool runs and the artifacts it produced. Slack reports that over 70% of code channels open and close within a single day.

faq.q: How is this different from using a coding agent in a private chat?
faq.a: A private agent chat is visible to one person, so review happens after the fact. Slack Code moves the same work into a channel where the plan, the diffs and the preview each get their own tab and every teammate sees them as they happen. The point is that a review and an approval step live where the work does.

explainer.tagline: Slack Code gives a coding agent its own project channel, so planning, diffs and sign-off all happen in front of the team.
explainer.whatIsIt: Mention a coding agent in Slack and Slack Code now spins up a dedicated code channel for that job. The channel pulls in the people who need to be there and splits the work across tabs: the conversation, the plan, the code diffs, and a live preview of what the agent built. Slack describes it as a place where "your team and its agents can plan, write, and review together".
explainer.howItWorks: Instead of rendering agent output as walls of text, code channels show diffs and previews as first-class surfaces. Changes flagged as high-stakes get routed to a named person for approval before they land. When the assignment is done the channel archives itself and stays searchable, keeping a record of the prompts, the agent's tool runs and the artifacts. Authentication and permissions ride on the existing Slack integration for whichever agent was tagged.
explainer.whyItMatters: Coding agents have mostly run in a private browser tab, so teammates only see the result once a pull request lands. Putting the run in a channel makes the intermediate work reviewable while it is still cheap to redirect, and it leaves an audit trail managers and security teams can search later. Slack reports that over 70% of code channels open and close within a single day, from idea to merged PR.
explainer.forWho: engineering teams already running coding agents in Slack

items.title: Antigravity IDE Extensions — Google's agent moves into VS Code and JetBrains
items.summary: Google put Antigravity inside VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains and Zed as one-click extensions that share context with the Antigravity desktop app and CLI. A companion release adds budget caps, token pools and audit logging for enterprises.

quickFacts.label: Supported IDEs
quickFacts.value: VS Code, Visual Studio (Preview), JetBrains, Zed

quickFacts.label: Install
quickFacts.value: One click from each IDE's extension marketplace

quickFacts.label: Individual access
quickFacts.value: Any Antigravity plan, including the free tier

quickFacts.label: Enterprise access
quickFacts.value: Eligible Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus plans

quickFacts.label: Enterprise sign-in
quickFacts.value: Workforce Identity Federation and Application Default Credentials

quickFacts.label: Admin controls
quickFacts.value: Sandboxing, budget caps, shared token pools, audit logging

faq.q: Is the Antigravity IDE extension free to use?
faq.a: Individual developers can install the Antigravity IDE extension on any Antigravity plan, including the free tier, by signing in with a Google account. Teams on Google Cloud reach it through Gemini Enterprise or Google Cloud project credentials instead, where JetBrains and Zed support is still marked Preview.

faq.q: How is the extension different from the Antigravity desktop app?
faq.a: Google built the Antigravity extensions as deliberately light integrations rather than a second agent hub — in its words, "lightweight, high-performance integrations" instead of trying to turn traditional editors into heavy multi-agent hubs. They are aimed at inspecting a code path, reading compiler diagnostics, or making a local edit, while the desktop app stays the place to orchestrate many agents.

faq.q: Can an admin stop Antigravity agents from browsing the web or running commands?
faq.a: Yes. Antigravity administrators can enforce workspace sandboxing and restrict browser or MCP server permissions so that, as Google puts it, agents "execute strictly within authorized environments". A single toggle also turns on full audit logging that captures prompts, agent tool executions and the artifacts an agent generates.

faq.q: Does Google train its models on code written through Antigravity at work?
faq.a: No. Google states that for enterprise use all Antigravity agent activity stays inside the customer's boundary under Google Cloud Terms of Service, and that "your code is never used to train base models". Inference runs through the customer's own Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform project rather than a consumer Google AI subscription.

faq.q: How do teams keep Antigravity from running up an unexpected bill?
faq.a: Antigravity administrators set monthly budget thresholds in Google Cloud Billing across projects, teams and individuals. Shared token pools stop purchased quota from sitting idle on one team while another runs dry, and organisations can opt into overages with strict caps so an active agent workflow is not cut off mid-task.

explainer.tagline: Google's agent-first coding platform now installs as a normal extension in the editor you already use.
explainer.whatIsIt: Antigravity extensions landed on 20 August 2026 for Visual Studio Code, Visual Studio (Preview), JetBrains IDEs including IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, CLion and Rider, and Zed. Each installs in one click from the editor's own marketplace. Until now Antigravity meant leaving your editor for Google's desktop app, its CLI or its SDK.
explainer.howItWorks: The extensions are intentionally thin. Google says it built "lightweight, high-performance integrations" rather than turning an editor into a second multi-agent hub, so the in-editor surface is for inspecting a code path, reading compiler diagnostics or making a local change. Multi-agent orchestration still runs in the wider Antigravity ecosystem, and the extension shares context with it, so a session you start in Zed is the same session the desktop app sees.
explainer.whyItMatters: Teams no longer have to adopt a new editor to try Google's coding agent, which removes the biggest reason to skip it. The enterprise release published the same day matters more for buyers: it puts Antigravity inside eligible Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus subscriptions and hands administrators sandboxing rules, browser and MCP permission limits, Google Cloud budget thresholds, shared token pools and one-toggle audit logging.
explainer.forWho: developers and platform teams evaluating Google's coding agent
explainer.tryIt: Install the Antigravity extension from your IDE's marketplace and sign in with a Google account.

items.title: LFM2.5-DSpark — Liquid AI's draft models decode up to 3.18x faster
items.summary: Liquid AI released DSpark draft models for three LFM2.5 checkpoints. Each is about 300M parameters and speeds up decoding through speculative decoding without changing the output: 2.67x on an H100 for LFM2.5-2.6B.

explainer.tagline: Three ~300M draft models that make Liquid AI's small on-device models decode two to three times faster, with identical output.
explainer.whatIsIt: DSpark adds speculative decoding to the LFM2.5 family. Liquid AI shipped draft checkpoints for LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct (295.7M parameters), LFM2.5-2.6B (327.7M) and LFM2.5-8B-A1B (327.7M). Because the drafter only proposes tokens that the target model then verifies, Liquid AI notes the emitted sequence is identical to baseline greedy decoding by construction, so benchmark accuracy does not move.
explainer.howItWorks: Each drafter stacks three pieces: a DFlash-style parallel backbone conditioned on context features that emits several candidate tokens at once, a lightweight sequential head that models the dependency between those tokens as a Markov chain, and a confidence-scheduled verifier that prunes low-confidence candidates before the target model checks them. Mean acceptance out of 10 drafted tokens runs 4.81 for the 2.6B target, 5.02 for the 1.2B and 6.95 for the 8B-A1B.
explainer.whyItMatters: Small on-device models are latency-bound, not quality-bound, and this is a free speed win for anyone already running LFM2.5. On an H100 through SGLang at batch size 1, LFM2.5-2.6B goes from 323 to 864 tokens per second, and LFM2.5-1.2B from 656 to 1,384. On an M4 Max MacBook through llama.cpp with Metal, LFM2.5-1.2B goes from 138 to 350 tokens per second. On the BFCL function-calling set, Liquid AI measures a 57% average latency cut for agent workloads.
explainer.forWho: developers running small models on phones, laptops and edge hardware

image.alt: Animated comparison of baseline decoding against LFM2.5-DSpark speculative decoding

items.title: Semantica v0.6.6 — security release hardens ingestion, adds CrewAI support
items.summary: Semantica v0.6.6 fixes a privately disclosed batch of vulnerabilities across backup, export, outbound requests and triplet-store backends, and hardens ingestion against SSRF. The same release adds CrewAI integration and graph retraction.

quickFacts.label: Project
quickFacts.value: Semantica — graph-native context store for AI agents

faq.q: Should I upgrade to Semantica v0.6.6 right away?
faq.a: The Semantica maintainers label v0.6.6 a security release and write that "upgrading is strongly recommended". It closes a privately disclosed batch of vulnerabilities rather than a single bug, and it arrived nine days after v0.6.5, which was also a security release. Anyone running Semantica on untrusted input should treat it as a priority upgrade.

faq.q: Which parts of Semantica were vulnerable?
faq.a: The v0.6.6 fixes span backup and restore, database export, outbound requests and the triplet-store backends. The ingestion path got the widest hardening: tarball path traversal, SQL injection, DNS-rebinding time-of-check-to-time-of-use races, stored XSS, SPARQL injection, header injection and credential leakage across redirects. An SSRF guard now also covers feed ingestion.

faq.q: What did Semantica v0.6.6 add besides the security fixes?
faq.a: Semantica v0.6.6 ships first-class CrewAI integration, retraction and purge operations on ContextGraph so facts can be pulled back out of a graph, a declared Semantica RDF vocabulary with deterministic entity and relationship IRIs, and timezone-aware timestamps throughout the export and provenance modules.

faq.q: Can agents now be told to forget something stored in Semantica?
faq.a: Yes, that is what the new ContextGraph retraction and purge operations in v0.6.6 are for. Retraction removes a fact from the active graph while the provenance record shows it was withdrawn; purge deletes it outright. Both matter for agent memory that has ingested data a user later asks to have deleted.

explainer.tagline: A strongly recommended security upgrade for the MIT-licensed knowledge-graph store behind a lot of agent memory.
explainer.whatIsIt: Version 0.6.6 of Semantica, the graph-native context and memory store for AI agents, closes a privately disclosed batch of vulnerabilities. The maintainers mark it a security release and state that "upgrading is strongly recommended". It follows v0.6.5, itself a security release, by nine days.
explainer.howItWorks: The fixes cluster around anything that touches outside data. Ingestion picked up guards for tarball path traversal, SQL injection, DNS-rebinding TOCTOU races, stored XSS, SPARQL injection, header injection and credential leakage across HTTP redirects, plus an SSRF guard applied to feed requests and a hardened GitPython clone surface in the repository ingestor. Backup and restore, database export and the triplet-store backends were patched alongside them.
explainer.whyItMatters: An agent memory store is the one component that deliberately swallows untrusted content — web pages, feeds, repositories, uploaded files — so an injection bug there reaches everything downstream. Beyond the patches, the release adds a CrewAI integration, ContextGraph retraction and purge, a declared RDF vocabulary with deterministic IRIs, and timezone-aware timestamps across export and provenance.
explainer.forWho: teams running Semantica as agent memory or a RAG knowledge graph

items.title: Simon Willison — ChatGPT search now scopes one query in six to a single site
items.summary: Simon Willison flags Promptwatch data showing ChatGPT's use of site:-scoped search queries jumped from 0.37% to 16.8% of all fanout queries on 8 August 2026, right after OpenAI updated GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT.

explainer.tagline: Promptwatch caught ChatGPT switching to domain-scoped search almost overnight, and Simon Willison explains what likely changed.
explainer.whatIsIt: Something changed in how ChatGPT searches the web on 8 August 2026, and Simon Willison's post walks through the evidence. Promptwatch measured the share of ChatGPT fanout queries that use the site: operator: it sat between 0.3% and 0.5% for weeks, dipped to 0.15% from 3 to 5 August, then jumped to 16.8% on 8 August and has stayed at 16-17%.
explainer.howItWorks: Fanout queries are the individual searches ChatGPT fires off behind one answer. Willison doubts OpenAI is literally telling the model to type site: in a query, and suggests the search tool signature now looks more like search(query, recency, domains), with the domain filter rendered as a site: clause. He ties the timing to OpenAI's 6 August note that it was updating GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT to be more reliable with facts and give more focused answers. Promptwatch also recorded average fanout queries per response rising from about 1.08 to 1.83 the same day, so scoped searches are being added rather than swapped in.
explainer.whyItMatters: Domain-scoped retrieval decides which sites an AI answer can cite at all, which is the whole game for anyone whose traffic now arrives through a chatbot. A separate Promptwatch report on 18 August found ChatGPT had sharply cut how often Reddit shows up in those searches; Willison notes he cannot confirm whether a system prompt was changed to discourage it.
explainer.forWho: publishers, SEO and GEO practitioners, and anyone tracking AI search citations

image.alt: Promptwatch, the AI-answer monitoring service behind the ChatGPT search data

items.title: Apple Messages plugin — ChatGPT can read and send texts on a Mac
items.summary: OpenAI's Apple Messages plugin lets ChatGPT read and search iMessage, SMS and RCS chats on a Mac and send replies through the Messages app. It runs in Codex and ChatGPT Work on the macOS desktop app, on all plans.

quickFacts.label: Not supported
quickFacts.value: Web, mobile, Codex CLI, IDE extension

faq.q: Which Macs support the ChatGPT Apple Messages plugin?
faq.a: The Apple Messages plugin runs only on Apple silicon (arm64) Macs with the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, so Intel machines are left out of this release. OpenAI also lists it as unavailable on ChatGPT for web, on mobile, in the Codex CLI and in the IDE extension, which makes a Mac desktop install the only route today.

faq.q: Do I need a paid ChatGPT plan for the Apple Messages plugin?
faq.a: The Apple Messages plugin is available on all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, so no paid upgrade is required. The real limit is the surface, not the subscription tier: the plugin works inside Codex and ChatGPT Work sessions, and OpenAI says it does not work in ordinary ChatGPT chats.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT send a text without asking me first?
faq.a: ChatGPT asks for approval before every send by default, showing both the message body and the recipients. You can pick 'Allow once' or 'Always allow sending to this chat', and a standing permission can be undone from Settings then Computer use. OpenAI documents one known issue: tasks running with Full access may skip the confirmation prompt.

faq.q: What kinds of messages can the Apple Messages plugin reach?
faq.a: The Apple Messages plugin reads and searches iMessage, SMS and RCS conversations in the Messages app on your Mac, and sends new messages through that same app. OpenAI is explicit that the plugin does not let you talk to ChatGPT remotely by texting it — the direction is one way, from a ChatGPT or Codex session out to Messages.

explainer.tagline: ChatGPT can now open your Mac's Messages app, search old threads and send a reply you approve.
explainer.whatIsIt: The Apple Messages plugin connects ChatGPT to the Messages app on a Mac, so it can read and search iMessage, SMS and RCS threads and send messages on your behalf. OpenAI shipped it on August 20, 2026 for the macOS desktop app. It arrives as an installable plugin rather than a change to ChatGPT itself.
explainer.howItWorks: Installation happens in the Plugins panel; once macOS permissions are granted, a fresh Codex or ChatGPT Work session can call the plugin to find, summarize, draft or send messages. Sending is gated by approval — ChatGPT shows the message and the recipients, and you choose 'Allow once' or 'Always allow sending to this chat'. A standing permission can be revoked under Settings then Computer use.
explainer.whyItMatters: Texting has been one of the last places an assistant could not reach without handing over a phone, and OpenAI closes that gap on the desktop instead of the phone. The trade is obvious: a tool that can read every chat and send on your behalf is a lot of trust, which is why per-message approval stays on by default. OpenAI flags one known issue — tasks set to Full access may not show the confirmation prompt.
explainer.forWho: Mac users of ChatGPT and Codex

items.title: Huzzah — an editor where you write pseudocode and an LLM fills in the code
items.summary: Huzzah is an experimental editor where you write pseudocode in .hz files and an LLM turns it into real source code. Each edit sends only the pseudocode diff as the prompt, and the pseudocode stays on disk as a record of intent.

explainer.tagline: Write pseudocode instead of a paragraph of English, and Huzzah syncs it into working code.
explainer.whatIsIt: Huzzah replaces the chat box with a pseudocode file. You write informal pseudocode in a .hz file — function calls, loops, conditionals and object shapes — and on save the editor generates the matching source code. Daniel Vaughn showed it on Hacker News on August 20, 2026, where it reached 165 points, and calls it a proof of concept that is still experimental.
explainer.howItWorks: When a .hz file changes, the editor captures the diff and sends only that diff to the model as the prompt, instead of restating the whole instruction. Source maps tie each piece of pseudocode back to the code it produced. Model access runs through Pi, so Anthropic, OpenAI or Google credentials all work, and the generated code runs in a Web Worker.
explainer.whyItMatters: Prompts to coding agents are long, imperative and thrown away when the session ends; the pseudocode Huzzah keeps is short, declarative and saved, so intent becomes something you edit rather than re-explain. Vaughn describes it as a condensed distillation of human intent. Hacker News readers split on it, with several asking how it differs from writing a spec or a careful commit message.
explainer.forWho: developers tired of writing long prompts
explainer.tryIt: git clone https://github.com/danielvaughn/hz && npm install && npm run dev

items.title: Vomit — a local model rewrites Claude Code's replies before you read them
items.summary: Vomit is a Go tool that hooks into Claude Code, buffers each reply and hands it to a local model to be rewritten in plainer language before it reaches the screen. Zach Ahn runs gpt-oss:20b for the rewriting pass.

explainer.tagline: Vomit pipes Claude Code's output through a small local model so the prose comes back plain.
explainer.whatIsIt: Vomit hooks into Claude Code and rewrites what the model says before you see it. Zach Ahn built it after deciding that Claude 5's default style — dense jargon and stretched metaphors — got in the way of the work, and describes the result as an art project that is new and lightly tested. The tool is written in Go and licensed GPL-3.0.
explainer.howItWorks: The tool buffers Claude Code's output, forwards each message to a local LLM, waits for the rewrite, then renders the new version through the MessageDisplay hook. Ahn uses gpt-oss:20b for that pass, so the rewriting stays on the machine. He notes some of the original phrasing still slips through, including plural pronouns like 'we'.
explainer.whyItMatters: Complaints about a model's writing style usually get answered with a longer system prompt; Vomit answers with a second model instead. The Hacker News thread reached 154 points and 271 comments, most of them arguing about whether the style is a training side effect of agentic coding work or a dialect you eventually learn to read.
explainer.forWho: Claude Code users
